title: Password attacks: online brute force, spraying, Windows credential dumping and offline cracking
intro: Password attacks end to end: brute-force and spray the services that authenticate users, reuse leaked and default credentials, dump the places Windows keeps credentials, then crack the hashes you capture offline with John the Ripper and Hashcat. Open any node for what it means and the commands behind it, or walk the offline crack step by step. Run noisy online attacks only against systems you are authorised to test, watch for account lockout, and keep every credential with the rest of the engagement notes.

phases.name: Remote service attacks
phases.blurb: Most network services authenticate with a username and password. Brute-force or spray them for a foothold, or to turn a cracked password into access.

nodes.label: The services worth attacking
nodes.detail: Networks run services that authenticate with a username and password: FTP, SMB, NFS, IMAP/POP3, SSH, MySQL/MSSQL, RDP, WinRM, VNC, Telnet, SMTP, LDAP. To drive a Windows host remotely the usual three are RDP (3389), WinRM (5985/5986) and SSH (22, uncommon on Windows, standard on Linux). Services are often left on default settings with password auth enabled, so they are worth a login attack, but online guessing is noisy and can lock accounts out.

children.label: WinRM
children.detail: Windows Remote Management is Microsoft's WS-Management implementation: XML web services over SOAP that bridge WBEM and WMI (and can reach DCOM) to manage Windows remotely. It is off by default on Windows 10/11 and must be enabled, so finding it open means someone turned it on. Default ports TCP 5985 (HTTP) and 5986 (HTTPS).

nodes.label: NetExec (nxc)
nodes.detail: NetExec (nxc, the maintained successor to CrackMapExec) sprays credentials across a protocol and reports what works. Install with apt. General form: netexec <proto> <ip> -u <user or list> -p <pass or list>. Protocols: nfs, ftp, ssh, winrm, smb, wmi, rdp, mssql, ldap, vnc. A (Pwn3d!) beside a WinRM or SMB hit means the account can most likely execute commands, not just log in.

children.label: Per-protocol help
children.detail: Each protocol has its own options; netexec <proto> -h prints them (netexec smb -h is huge: shares, --sam, --lsa, --ntds, spidering, command execution). The target can be an IP, range, CIDR, hostname, file of targets, or an Nmap/Nessus export.

nodes.label: Evil-WinRM (shell)
nodes.detail: Once WinRM creds work, Evil-WinRM opens an interactive shell over PowerShell Remoting (MS-PSRP). Install it as a gem. It is the standard way to use a WinRM foothold.

nodes.label: SSH (Hydra, then log in)
nodes.detail: SSH (TCP 22) secures the channel with symmetric encryption (AES, 3DES; the key agreed by Diffie-Hellman), asymmetric key authentication (a private key, often unprotected, is as good as a login) and hashing for integrity. Brute the password with Hydra, throttling to about four tasks because SSH configs cap parallel logins, then connect with the OpenSSH client.

nodes.label: RDP (Hydra, then xfreerdp)
nodes.detail: RDP (TCP 3389) gives a full remote desktop. Brute it with Hydra, but keep the task count low (-t 1 to 4, -W to wait): RDP dislikes parallel connections and the module is experimental. Hydra may report an account as "valid but not active for remote desktop" when the password is right but the account lacks RDP rights. Connect with xfreerdp (or Remmina).

nodes.label: SMB (Hydra / Metasploit)
nodes.detail: SMB (TCP 445, file and printer sharing; CIFS is the dialect, Samba the Linux implementation) authenticates too. Hydra can brute it, but an old THC-Hydra fails SMBv3 with "invalid reply from target"; fall back to Metasploit's auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_login. With valid creds, list shares with netexec --shares and browse them with smbclient.

children.label: Metasploit smb_login
children.detail: When Hydra cannot speak SMBv3, use the smb_login scanner: set USER_FILE, PASS_FILE and RHOSTS, then run. STOP_ON_SUCCESS and a low THREADS keep it tidy; a Success line confirms the pair.

phases.name: Spraying, stuffing & defaults
phases.blurb: One password against many accounts, reused credentials against new services, and the credentials nobody changed.

nodes.label: Password spraying
nodes.detail: Spraying tries a single password across many usernames, the opposite of hammering one account, so it stays under lockout thresholds (one guess per account per round). It pays off where new accounts get a standard password such as ChangeMe123! that someone never changed. For Active Directory use NetExec or Kerbrute; for web apps, Burp.

nodes.label: Credential stuffing
nodes.detail: Stuffing replays username:password pairs stolen from one service against others, betting on reuse across email, social and enterprise logins. Hydra's -C flag takes a combined user:pass file (one pair per line) rather than separate lists.

nodes.label: Default credentials
nodes.detail: Routers, firewalls, databases and appliances ship with default credentials that are meant to be changed at setup but often are not. The defaultcreds-cheat-sheet tool looks them up by product (creds search <vendor>); product documentation and router lists are the other sources. Collect the finds into a user:pass list and feed Hydra.

children.label: Router defaults
children.detail: Routers are less likely to be left on defaults because they are critical, but internal test routers often are. Common brand/IP/username/password combinations are in the router-defaults table below; the admin panel usually sits at the gateway IP.

phases.name: Windows credentials: dump & crack
phases.blurb: Where Windows keeps credentials: dump the SAM hives, LSASS memory, Credential Manager vaults and the domain's NTDS.dit, then crack the NT and DCC2 hashes, or pass them.

nodes.label: The authentication flow
nodes.detail: On an interactive logon, WinLogon (the trusted process that owns login, lock/unlock and password changes) launches LogonUI, which collects credentials through a credential provider (a COM DLL). WinLogon hands them to LSASS, which runs them through an authentication package and checks them against the SAM (local) or Active Directory (domain) via LSALogonUser. The LSA is the protected subsystem that authenticates users, holds local security policy, and maps names to SIDs.

children.label: LSASS (the gatekeeper)
children.detail: The Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (%SystemRoot%\System32\lsass.exe) enforces local security policy, authenticates users and forwards audit logs. Its Negotiate function picks NTLM or Kerberos. Because it holds live credential material in memory, LSASS is a prime dumping target (Mimikatz).

children.label: Authentication packages
children.detail: Authentication packages are DLLs LSASS loads to do the checks: Lsasrv, Msv1_0 (local/NTLM), Samsrv (SAM), Kerberos, Netlogon, Ntdsa (AD, DCs only). They are listed in the authentication-packages table below.

nodes.label: SAM database
nodes.detail: The Security Account Manager stores local account credentials as LM or NTLM hashes in the registry. The file is %SystemRoot%\system32\config\SAM, mounted at HKLM\SAM, and reading it needs SYSTEM privileges. SYSKEY partially encrypts it on disk with a system boot key (held in HKLM\SYSTEM), so you need both to decrypt the hashes. A workgroup host keeps users locally in SAM; a domain host validates against AD's ntds.dit instead.

nodes.label: Credential Manager, NTDS & DPAPI
nodes.detail: Beyond SAM, Windows keeps credentials in several stores. Credential Manager holds per-user saved logins in the Credential Locker (AppData\Local\Microsoft\Credentials), DPAPI-encrypted. NTDS.dit is the Active Directory database on Domain Controllers (user, group and computer accounts with hashes, plus GPOs), synced across DCs except RODCs. DPAPI is the per-user encrypt/decrypt API behind saved browser and Outlook passwords, RDP credentials and Credential Manager entries.

nodes.label: Dump the hives (reg.exe)
nodes.detail: With local admin you can back up the registry hives and crack offline, with no live session to maintain. SAM holds the hashes, SYSTEM the boot key that decrypts them, SECURITY the LSA secrets (DCC2, cleartext, DPAPI keys). For local users you only need SAM and SYSTEM; take SECURITY too for cached domain credentials. Run reg.exe from an elevated cmd.exe.

children.label: Which hive holds what
children.detail: SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY each play a part in dumping and cracking; the registry-hives table below says what each one holds and why you need it.

nodes.label: Exfiltrate with smbserver
nodes.detail: Move the saved hives to your attack host over SMB with Impacket's smbserver: start a share, then use the Windows move command to push the files. Pass -smb2support, or modern Windows (SMBv1 disabled by default) will refuse to connect.

nodes.label: secretsdump (extract hashes)
nodes.detail: Impacket's secretsdump reads the three hives and prints the local SAM hashes as uid:rid:lmhash:nthash, plus cached domain logons and LSA secrets (DPAPI machine/user keys, NL$KM). It fetches the boot key first to decrypt the SAM. Copy the NT hash (the fourth field, after the LM hash) for each user into a file, noting which hash is whose.

nodes.label: Crack NT hashes (-m 1000)
nodes.detail: Most modern Windows stores passwords as NT hashes; older systems (pre-Vista / Server 2008) may still hold weaker LM hashes. Put the NT hashes in a file and crack with Hashcat mode 1000. NTLM is unsalted and fast (megahashes per second), so a wordlist with rules clears weak passwords quickly. Reuse what cracks, people repeat passwords across systems.

nodes.label: Crack DCC2 hashes (-m 2100)
nodes.detail: SECURITY yields DCC2 (MS Cache v2) hashes, local copies of domain credentials cached for offline logon ($DCC2$10240#user#...). Hashcat mode 2100. They use PBKDF2, so they crack roughly 800 times slower than NTLM and cannot be used for pass-the-hash, which means a strong one is often uncrackable inside an engagement window.

nodes.label: Decrypt DPAPI secrets
nodes.detail: The DPAPI machine and user keys from SECURITY unlock DPAPI blobs: saved browser and Outlook passwords, RDP credentials and Credential Manager entries. Decrypt them with Impacket's dpapi, Mimikatz, or remotely with DonPAPI. Mimikatz's dpapi::chrome pulls the AES key and reads the saved login directly.

nodes.label: Dump remotely (NetExec)
nodes.detail: With credentials that hold local admin, you can dump over SMB instead of touching disk: --sam for the local SAM hashes, --lsa for LSA secrets (which may expose service and cached credentials in cleartext). NetExec writes the loot to its logs for later cracking.

nodes.label: Attacking LSASS (memory dump)
nodes.detail: LSASS caches the credentials of every active logon session in memory, so dumping its process memory and parsing the dump offline yields hashes, and sometimes cleartext, without ever cracking the SAM. Take the same offline-first approach as the hives: snapshot LSASS, pull the dump to your box, parse it there. Modern AV flags the common dump methods as malicious, so expect to deal with that.

children.label: Dump LSASS memory
children.detail: Two methods built into Windows. With an interactive desktop: Task Manager, Processes tab, right-click Local Security Authority Process, Create dump file, which writes lsass.DMP to %temp%. From a shell: rundll32 calls comsvcs.dll's MiniDump function, which needs the LSASS PID first (tasklist /svc, or Get-Process lsass). Run it from an elevated prompt. The comsvcs route is faster and needs no GUI, but AV usually recognises it.

children.label: Exfiltrate the dump (smbserver)
children.detail: Pull lsass.dmp back to the attack host with Impacket's smbserver, exactly as with the SAM hives: start a share, then move the file over SMB. Keep -smb2support so modern Windows (SMBv1 disabled) will connect. Parsing offline keeps time on the target short.

children.label: Parse with pypykatz, then crack
children.detail: pypykatz is Mimikatz reimplemented in Python, so it parses an LSASS dump offline on a Linux host (Mimikatz is Windows-only). pypykatz lsa minidump <dump> walks each logon session and prints its secrets: MSV (the NT and SHA1 hashes), WDIGEST (cleartext on older Windows), Kerberos (tickets and keys) and the DPAPI masterkey. The secret types are in the table below. Crack the NT hash with Hashcat mode 1000.

nodes.label: Attacking Credential Manager (Windows Vault)
nodes.detail: Credential Manager (since Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2) lets users and apps save credentials for other systems, sites and services. They live in encrypted vault/locker folders under the user and system profiles; each vault's Policy.vpol holds AES-128/256 keys that are themselves protected by DPAPI, and on newer Windows those master keys are guarded by Credential Guard in VBS memory enclaves. Two kinds are stored: Web Credentials (websites, legacy IE/Edge) and Windows Credentials (domain logons, network shares, services such as OneDrive). Enumerate them, reuse them without the password, or decrypt them.

children.label: Enumerate (cmdkey)
children.detail: cmdkey /list prints the current user's saved credentials with their Target (the resource or account), Type (Generic or Domain Password), User, and persistence (an entry marked Local machine persistence survives reboots). A WindowsLive:target=virtualapp/didlogical entry is an internal Microsoft-account ID you can ignore; a Domain:interactive=HOST\user entry is a reusable interactive domain logon.

children.label: Reuse without the password (runas /savecred)
children.detail: When cmdkey shows a Domain:interactive credential, you do not need its plaintext: runas /savecred spends the saved credential to launch a process as that user. Confirm with whoami in the new shell. A quick path from a stored credential to impersonation.

children.label: Decrypt the plaintext (mimikatz / DPAPI)
children.detail: To recover the actual password, decrypt the vault. Mimikatz pulls saved credentials straight from LSASS with sekurlsa::credman (run privilege::debug first), or decrypts the vault files by hand with its dpapi module using the DPAPI master key. SharpDPAPI, LaZagne and DonPAPI do the same, DonPAPI remotely.

children.label: Export the vault (keymgr.dll)
children.detail: The GUI route: rundll32 keymgr.dll,KRShowKeyMgr opens the Stored User Names and Passwords window, where a vault exports to a password-protected .crd file (also doable from Control Panel) that imports on another Windows host. The vault and locker folder paths are in the table below.

nodes.label: Active Directory: dump NTDS.dit
nodes.detail: On a domain-joined network the prize is the Domain Controller's NTDS.dit (%SystemRoot%\NTDS\ntds.dit, "directory information tree"), the Active Directory database holding every domain account's username and password hash. Capture it, with the SYSTEM hive for the boot key as with the SAM, and the whole domain falls. Getting there: build and validate usernames, guess a password, reach the DC as an admin, then copy and extract the database. These attacks need a foothold on the internal network and are noisy.

children.label: Build & validate usernames
children.detail: Usernames follow a convention (jdoe, jane.doe, doe.jane), often visible in an email address (jdoe@corp means jdoe) or scraped from the company site and social media. Turn real names into candidates by hand or with username-anarchy, then confirm which actually exist with Kerbrute's userenum against the DC, so you only spray real accounts. The conventions are in the table below.

children.label: Guess passwords (NetExec)
children.detail: With valid usernames, brute or spray them against the DC over SMB with NetExec. Mind account lockout (not enabled by default in AD, so many environments are exposed to this); every attempt logs Event ID 4776 on the DC, so it is far from quiet.

children.label: Reach the DC & check rights
children.detail: Log in to the DC with the working credential, Evil-WinRM gives a PowerShell session. Copying NTDS.dit needs local admin (Administrators) or Domain Admin, so check your rights with net localgroup and net user <user> (look for Domain Admins or Administrators in the memberships).

children.label: Copy NTDS.dit (shadow copy)
children.detail: NTDS.dit is locked while AD runs, so copy it out of a Volume Shadow Copy instead: vssadmin creates a snapshot of C: that can be read live, and you copy ntds.dit from the shadow volume. Grab the SYSTEM hive too, the hashes are encrypted with its boot key and will not decrypt without it.

children.label: Extract the hashes
children.detail: Move NTDS.dit and SYSTEM to the attack host over an smbserver share, then dump with Impacket's secretsdump. Faster: skip the manual copy entirely and let NetExec run the whole VSS-and-dump remotely with its ntdsutil module. Either way you get every domain hash, krbtgt and the machine accounts included.

children.label: Crack, or Pass-the-Hash
children.detail: Crack the NT hashes with Hashcat mode 1000. If one will not crack, you can still use it: Pass-the-Hash authenticates with the hash itself over NTLM (username:hash instead of username:password), so an uncracked Administrator hash is still a login. Evil-WinRM takes -H for exactly this; more on PtH in the AD enumeration and attacks material.

phases.name: Identify the hash
phases.blurb: The format has to match, or nothing cracks. Guess it, confirm it, then tell the tool: --format for John, -m for Hashcat.

nodes.label: An unknown hash
nodes.detail: Hashes often arrive with no label, and even the tools cannot always name them with certainty. 193069ceb0461e1d40d216e32c79c704 is a 32-hex-character string that could be MD5, NTLM, LM, RIPEMD-128 and a dozen others. Narrowing it down is part of the job; the context it came from is often the deciding clue. (This particular one is RIPEMD-128.)

nodes.label: hashID (-j John, -m Hashcat)
nodes.detail: hashID checks a hash against a built-in list and suggests formats. -j adds the matching John format name beside each guess, -m adds the Hashcat mode number, so you can go straight to --format or -m. It usually returns several candidates, not one, so weigh them against where the hash came from.

nodes.label: Sample-hash references
nodes.detail: When a tool will not commit, compare against known examples. John's own sample-hash documentation and the PentestMonkey cheat sheet list example hashes next to the John format name. Hashcat hosts a comprehensive example-hashes table that does the same for mode numbers. Match your hash by shape, then look up the value.

nodes.label: Tell the tool the format
nodes.detail: Once you know it, name it so the tool stops guessing. John takes --format=<name> (--list=formats lists them all); Hashcat takes -m <mode> (hashcat --help lists every mode and its ID). The two reference tables below pair common formats with the John value and the Hashcat mode.

phases.name: Build a targeted wordlist
phases.blurb: A generic list is often blocked or exhausted. Mutate words that fit the target, and harvest the target's own language.

nodes.label: How users beat a password policy
nodes.detail: Policies force length and character classes (typically 8+ characters with an uppercase, a lowercase, a number and a symbol), but people meet them predictably. They capitalise the first letter (Password), append numbers (Password123), a year (Password2022) or a month (Password02), end with an exclamation mark (Password2022!), and leetspeak the letters (P@ssw0rd2022!). Most passwords are ten characters or fewer, and a forced rotation usually just bumps a digit or swaps the month. Knowing this, you mutate a small set of likely base words rather than brute-forcing blind.

children.label: Seed words from OSINT
children.detail: The best base words come from the target: the company name, the region and industry, and personal details, pet and family names, hobbies, sports, interests. Basic OSINT (the Corporate Recon material) turns these up. Pick terms of at least five characters; a base word plus a year and a symbol already fills a ten-character policy.

nodes.label: Generate mutations (hashcat --stdout -r)
nodes.detail: A rule file tells Hashcat how to transform each input word, one rule per line. Run the base list through the rules with --stdout to print the mutations instead of cracking, and save a custom wordlist. The rule functions are in the table below: : does nothing, c capitalises, so0 replaces o with 0, sa@ replaces a with @, $! appends an exclamation mark, and rules combine on a line (c so0). A single word like password through a fifteen-line custom.rule yields password, Password, p@ssw0rd, P@ssw0rd!, and so on.

nodes.label: Prebuilt rulesets (best64)
nodes.detail: Both tools ship rulesets you do not have to write. best64.rule is the usual first reach: 64 common transformations that crack a surprising share of passwords. Hashcat's live under /usr/share/hashcat/rules (best64, rockyou-30000, dive and more); John has its own in john.conf. Cracking is a guessing game, so narrow it with what you know, policy, company, region, industry, keywords, unless the password simply leaked.

nodes.label: Harvest a site with CeWL
nodes.detail: CeWL spiders a company's website and collects the words it uses into a list, which you then feed through your rules. The result is far likelier to hold an employee's base word than a generic list. Set the spider depth with -d, the minimum word length with -m, store words in lowercase with --lowercase, and write the output with -w.

phases.name: John the Ripper
phases.blurb: The CPU cracker. Open-source since 1996; reach for it on boxes without a GPU, for odd formats, and for its *2john file converters.

nodes.label: Use the jumbo build
nodes.detail: John the Ripper (JtR, or john) recovers passwords from hashes through dictionary and brute-force-style attacks. The community "jumbo" build is the one to use: performance optimisations, multilingual word lists, 64-bit support, and far more hash formats than the core release. The *2john converters come with it.

nodes.label: john --single
nodes.detail: Single crack mode is rule-based and best against Linux credentials. It builds candidates from the victim's own data, the username, home directory name and GECOS fields (full name, room, phone), then runs them through a large set of common string-mangling rules. A user named Bob Smith might use Smith1, so single mode tries exactly that. Feed it a passwd-format file and it reads the identity fields itself.

nodes.label: john --wordlist=
nodes.detail: Wordlist mode is a dictionary attack: every entry in one or more plain-text wordlists, one candidate per line. Separate several with commas. Add --rules to mutate each word (append digits, capitalise, add symbols) and reach passwords the raw list misses. The workhorse once single mode is exhausted.

nodes.label: john --incremental
nodes.detail: Incremental mode is a smart brute force. It generates candidates from a statistical (Markov) model so likelier passwords come first, which makes it far more efficient than naive brute force, but it is still the most exhaustive and slowest mode. The character sets and length limits live in john.conf; name a charset directly (--incremental=ASCII) or build your own custom.chr. Narrow the set and length to keep it tractable.

children.label: Predefined charsets
children.detail: john.conf ships several: Custom ($JOHN/custom.chr), UTF8 (196 characters), Latin1 (CP1252, 203 characters), and ASCII (95 characters, MaxLen 13). Pick one with --incremental=<name>, or make a custom.chr for special characters and specific patterns. A tighter set and shorter MaxLen finish sooner.

phases.name: Hashcat
phases.blurb: The GPU cracker. Open-source since 2015, Linux/Windows/macOS; the fastest route when you have a real GPU and a supported hash.

nodes.label: hashcat -a <mode> -m <type>
nodes.detail: Hashcat cracks a wide variety of hashes with strong GPU support. The general form is hashcat -a <attack mode> -m <hash type> <hashes> [wordlist, rule, mask...]. -a picks the attack (0 dictionary, 3 mask), -m picks the hash type by ID, <hashes> is a string or a file of same-type hashes, and the rest depends on the attack. In a VM without a GPU it crawls, so a CPU box is often faster with John.

children.label: Finding the hash type (-m)
children.detail: Hashcat supports hundreds of hash types, each with a numeric ID. hashcat --help prints the full list (e.g. 0 MD5, 100 SHA1, 1400 SHA2-256, 1000 NTLM, 2100 DCC2). Confirm an unknown one against the Hashcat example-hashes table, or with hashid -m. The Hashcat modes table below lists the common ones.

nodes.label: Dictionary attack (-a 0)
nodes.detail: The dictionary attack takes a wordlist and tries each word against the hash until it cracks or the list runs out. Identify the hash type first (an MD5 like e3e3ec5831ad5e7288241960e5d4fdb8 is mode 0), then point hashcat at rockyou. The first thing to try.

nodes.label: Rules (-r)
nodes.detail: A wordlist alone is often not enough. Rules apply modifications to each candidate, appending numbers, substituting leet characters and more, to generate many more guesses from the same list. Hashcat's rule files live in /usr/share/hashcat/rules; best64.rule (64 standard modifications) is the usual first reach, with bigger sets like rockyou-30000.rule and dive.rule when it is not enough. Append -r <ruleset> to a dictionary attack.

nodes.label: Mask attack (-a 3)
nodes.detail: A mask attack is a brute force where you define the keyspace explicitly, so you try only the shapes a password could take instead of every combination. A mask is a sequence of charset symbols. To try an uppercase letter, four lowercase, a digit, then a symbol, the mask is ?u?l?l?l?l?d?s. Far faster than blind brute force when you know the shape; the symbol table is below.

children.label: Custom charsets (-1 to -4)
children.detail: Beyond the built-in symbols, define up to four custom sets with -1, -2, -3 and -4, then reference them in the mask as ?1, ?2, ?3 and ?4. For example -1 ?l?d builds a set of lowercase letters and digits, used in a mask as ?1. Handy when a policy mixes a known subset of characters.

phases.name: Protected files & archives
phases.blurb: Encrypted files, keys and archives crack too: a *2john script extracts a hash, then John or Hashcat does the rest.

nodes.label: Hunt for encrypted files
nodes.detail: First find what is worth cracking. Encrypted files take many extensions (FileInfo lists hundreds); search the filesystem for the common document and archive types and strip the noise. An unfamiliar extension is a search-engine lookup away. Encryption at rest is often neglected, so sensitive documents, statements and contracts turn up unencrypted or weakly protected.
cmd: for ext in $(echo ".xls .xls* .doc .doc* .pdf .pp* .od* .zip .rar .7z .kdbx"); do echo "\nExt: $ext"; find / -name "*$ext" 2>/dev/null | grep -v "lib\|fonts\|share\|core"; done

nodes.label: SSH keys (ssh2john)
nodes.detail: SSH private keys have no fixed extension, so find them by content: the header line -----BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY-----. Old PEM keys announced encryption in the header (Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED); modern OpenSSH keys look identical whether encrypted or not, so test one with ssh-keygen -yf, which prints the public key for an unencrypted key and prompts for a passphrase for an encrypted one. An encrypted key becomes a hash with ssh2john, then crack it.

nodes.label: Office & PDF (office2john, pdf2john)
nodes.detail: Password-protected Office documents and PDFs are everywhere. office2john extracts a hash from any common Office format, pdf2john does the same for a PDF; the cracking step is identical to any other hash. Swap one script for the other depending on the file.

nodes.label: ZIP archives (zip2john)
nodes.detail: A password-protected ZIP cracks like anything else once zip2john pulls the hash out. The extracted hash names the archive and the file inside it ($pkzip2$...); feed it to John with a wordlist, then --show the result.

nodes.label: OpenSSL-encrypted archives (GZIP)
nodes.detail: Not every protected file advertises it: a format that has no native password protection (a TAR or GZIP) may be wrapped with openssl instead. file tells you the truth, reporting "openssl enc'd data with salted password". There is no hash to extract, so crack it by brute force: a for loop that tries each wordlist entry as the key and only succeeds when the decrypt-and-extract works. The gzip and tar errors from wrong keys are safe to ignore; a new file in the directory means a hit.
cmd: for i in $(cat rockyou.txt); do openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -d -in GZIP.gzip -k $i 2>/dev/null | tar xz 2>/dev/null; done

nodes.label: BitLocker drives (bitlocker2john)
nodes.detail: BitLocker is Microsoft's full-disk encryption (AES-128 or AES-256), and virtual drives (.vhd) are sometimes used to lock personal files on company devices. bitlocker2john reads the volume and emits four hashes: the first two are the user password, the last two the 48-digit recovery key. The recovery key is random and not worth guessing, so crack the password hash, the one starting $bitlocker$0$. Hashcat mode 22100 handles it; AES makes it slow.

children.label: Mounting the cracked drive (loop devices)
children.detail: Cracking the password is only half of it; mounting the drive is where people get stuck, because a .vhd is a whole virtual disk, not a single volume. The BitLocker-encrypted filesystem lives in a partition inside the disk, so dislocker has to point at that partition, not the disk. losetup -f -P attaches the .vhd as a loop device (/dev/loop0) and -P exposes each partition as /dev/loop0p1, /dev/loop0p2 and so on. Guessing the partition fails loudly: /dev/loop0 (the whole disk) gives "Cannot parse volume header", and a partition that does not exist (/dev/loop0p2 here) gives "No such file or directory". So list the partitions with fdisk -lu /dev/loop0 and read off the NTFS one (here /dev/loop0p1). Point dislocker at it with the cracked password; it decrypts the partition to a virtual clear-text file named dislocker-file, which you then mount as an ordinary loop filesystem and browse. Unmount both mounts when you are done.

phases.name: Collect
phases.blurb: Read the results back, and handle them as sensitive engagement loot.

nodes.label: --show the cracked passwords
nodes.detail: Both tools store cracked results. john --show reads them back reliably; hashcat --show prints them from the potfile (re-run with the same -m and hash file). Note which credential came from which host and account, keep the loot with the rest of the engagement notes, treat cracked passwords as sensitive, and feed them back into spraying, stuffing and lateral movement where the scope allows.

workflow.title: Identify
workflow.text: Name the format with hashID (-j for John, -m for Hashcat) and the sample-hash references.

workflow.title: Build the wordlist
workflow.text: Mutate target-specific base words with rules (hashcat --stdout -r), and harvest the site with CeWL.

workflow.title: Extract (if a file)
workflow.text: Protected file, key or archive? Run the matching *2john script (ssh2john, office2john, zip2john...) to get a crackable hash.

workflow.title: Dictionary + rules
workflow.text: Run a dictionary attack with your wordlist, then again with rules: john --rules, or hashcat -a 0 -r.

workflow.title: Mask / brute force
workflow.text: Known shape? Run a mask attack (hashcat -a 3) or John's incremental brute force, narrowed to a charset and length.

workflow.title: Collect
workflow.text: Read cracked passwords back with --show and record where each one came from.

references.title: Hashcat rule functions
references.intro: The common rule functions used to mutate a word, one rule per line; combine several on a line (c so0). The full set is in the Hashcat rule-based attack documentation.
rows: Capitalise the first letter, lowercase the rest
Replace every X with Y (e.g. so0, sa@)
Append the ! character at the end
Append the character X at the end
Prepend the character X at the start

references.title: Windows authentication packages
references.intro: The DLLs LSASS loads to perform authentication checks. Filter by package or role.
rows: LSA server: enforces security policy and manages the LSA's security packages; holds the Negotiate function that picks NTLM or Kerberos
Authentication package for local-machine logons that need no custom authentication (NTLM)
Security Accounts Manager: stores local accounts, enforces local policy, exposes the SAM APIs
Kerberos authentication package loaded by the LSA
Directory System Agent: manages the AD database (ntds.dit), LDAP queries and DC replication; loaded on Domain Controllers only

references.title: Registry hives for hash dumping
references.intro: Back these up with reg.exe (local admin) and crack offline. Filter by hive or description.
rows: Password hashes for local accounts (LM/NTLM); crackable once decrypted
The system boot key that encrypts the SAM; required to decrypt the hashes
LSA secrets: cached domain credentials (DCC2), cleartext passwords, DPAPI keys and more

references.title: What pypykatz pulls from LSASS
references.intro: The secret types pypykatz (and Mimikatz) extract from a logon session in an LSASS dump. Filter by secret.
rows: The account's NT and SHA1 password hashes (crack the NT with -m 1000)
Cleartext password on Windows <= 8 / Server <= 2012; disabled by default on modern Windows
Cached tickets, encryption keys and PINs, reusable against other domain-joined systems
The logon session's masterkey, which decrypts that user's DPAPI secrets (browser, RDP, Credential Manager)

references.title: Credential Manager vault folders
references.intro: Where Windows keeps the encrypted vault and credential-locker folders. Each holds a DPAPI-protected Policy.vpol with the AES keys that encrypt the stored credentials. Filter by path.

references.title: AD username conventions
references.intro: How organisations turn a real name into a username. Knowing the convention (from an email address or a leaked document) means you spray real accounts instead of guessing. Filter by convention.

references.title: Router default credentials
references.intro: A sample of common factory logins; internal test routers are the ones most likely left unchanged. Filter by brand.

references.title: John --format reference
references.intro: A selection of the hundreds of formats John supports. Pass the value to --format so John does not have to guess. Filter by name, value or description.
rows: bfegg hashes used in Eggdrop IRC bots
hdaa password hashes used in Openwall GNU/Linux
MS Cache (domain cached credentials) password hashes
MS Cache v2 (domain cached credentials 2) password hashes
NETLMv2 (NT LAN Manager version 2) password hashes
NETNTLMv2 (NT LAN Manager version 2) password hashes
PHPass-MD5 (Portable PHP password hashing framework) hashes

references.title: Hashcat mode reference
references.intro: Common Hashcat hash types and their mode IDs for -m. hashcat --help prints the full list of hundreds. Filter by mode, name or category.

references.title: Hashcat mask charsets
references.intro: The built-in character sets a mask (-a 3) is built from. Combine the symbols to describe a password's shape; define your own with -1 to -4.

references.title: John file converters (*2john)
references.intro: The headline *2john tools. Each reads a protected or encrypted file and writes a John-format hash: <tool> <file> > file.hash. Many more ship with the jumbo build; locate '*2john*' lists them.
